stem: A 23-year-old man is incidentally found to have fructose in the urine during evaluation for a life insurance policy.  He is asymptomatic and has no other medical conditions.  Genetic testing confirms a hereditary defect in fructose metabolism.  Continued metabolism of dietary fructose in this patient depends on the activity of which of the following enzymes?​‌​‌‌‌‌‌‌​‌‌​‌​​​‌‌​​‌​​​‌‌‌‌​​‌‌‌‌‌‌‌​​‌‌‌​‌‌​‌‌​​‌‌‌​​​‌​‌‌​‌​‌‌​​‌‌​​‌‌​​‌‌​‌‌​‌‌​‌‌‌‌​‌​‌​​​‌‌‌‌‌‌​​‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌​‌​​​​​‌‌‌​​​​‌‌‌‌‌​​​​‌‌​​‌‌​‌‌‌​​​‌​​‌​​​‌​​‌​‌​​​​​‌​‌​​‌‌‌‌​‌​‌​​‌‌‌‌‌​​​​‌​​​​‌​‌​​​‌‌​‌​​​​‌‌‌​​‌​‌‌​​‌‌‌‌​​‌‌​​‌‌‌​‌‌​‌​‌​‌​‌‌​‌‌‌‌‌​​​‌‌‌‌‌​​​​​‌​​​​​‌​‌​‌​‌​​‌​‌​​​​​‌​​‌​‌‌​‌‌​​‌‌​‌​‌‌‌‌​​‌‌​‌‌​‌‌​​​‌​‌​​​​​​​
explanation:
This patient has essential fructosuria, an autosomal recessive condition caused by fructokinase deficiency.  Dietary fructose (derived from fruit, honey, and sucrose) is absorbed across the intestinal brush border via GLUT5.  In the liver, kidney, and small intestine, fructokinase phosphorylates it to fructose 1-phosphate, which aldolase B cleaves into dihydroxyacetone phosphate and glyceraldehyde.  These metabolites enter glycolysis downstream of phosphofructokinase-1 and therefore escape the principal regulatory step of glycolysis.

In patients who have fructokinase deficiency, alternative tissues (eg, skeletal muscle, adipose) use hexokinase to phosphorylate fructose to fructose 6-phosphate, which can enter glycolysis directly or be isomerized to glucose-6-phosphate for entry into other metabolic pathways (eg, glycogen synthesis).  Because hexokinase has a far lower affinity for fructose than for glucose, a portion of the ingested fructose load remains unmetabolized and is excreted as free fructose in the urine.

The disorder is benign because fructose is not trapped as fructose 1-phosphate; any fructose 6-phosphate formed by hexokinase is freely metabolized onward, and the unphosphorylated remainder is nontoxic and readily filtered, so no organ injury occurs.  Diagnosis is typically incidental when urinalysis shows a positive urine reducing-substance test with a negative glucose oxidase dipstick.

(Choice A)  Aldolase B acts on fructose 1-phosphate, a metabolite that is never formed when fructokinase is absent.  Aldolase B deficiency (hereditary fructose intolerance) also produces fructosuria but presents in infancy (when fructose or sucrose is first introduced) with vomiting, hypoglycemia, and hepatic dysfunction caused by toxic accumulation of fructose 1-phosphate.

(Choice B)  Aldose reductase reduces glucose to sorbitol, which is then oxidized by sorbitol dehydrogenase to fructose (polyol pathway).  This process generates fructose rather than metabolizing it and becomes significant in chronic hyperglycemia.

(Choice D)  UDP-galactose 4-epimerase is involved in the metabolism of galactose; it does not play a role in fructose metabolism.

Educational objective:Essential fructosuria is a benign disorder caused by fructokinase deficiency.  Because fructose is never trapped as fructose 1-phosphate, no tissue injury occurs; fructose is instead slowly phosphorylated by hexokinase, and the portion that escapes metabolism is excreted in the urine (positive urine reducing-substance, negative glucose oxidase dipstick).​‌​‌‌‌‌‌‌​‌‌​‌​​​‌‌​​‌​​​‌‌‌‌​​‌‌‌‌‌‌‌​​‌‌‌​‌‌​‌‌​​‌‌‌​​​‌​‌‌​‌​‌‌​​‌‌​​‌‌​​‌‌​‌‌​‌‌​‌‌‌‌​‌​‌​​​‌‌‌‌‌‌​​‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌​‌​​​​​‌‌‌​​​​‌‌‌‌‌​​​​‌‌​​‌‌​‌‌‌​​​‌​​‌​​​‌​​‌​‌​​​​​‌​‌​​‌‌‌‌​‌​‌​​‌‌‌‌‌​​​​‌​​​​‌​‌​​​‌‌​‌​​​​‌‌‌​​‌​‌‌​​‌‌‌‌​​‌‌​​‌‌‌​‌‌​‌​‌​‌​‌‌​‌‌‌‌‌​​​‌‌‌‌‌​​​​​‌​​​​​‌​‌​‌​‌​​‌​‌​​​​​‌​​‌​‌‌​‌‌​​‌‌​‌​‌‌‌‌​​‌‌​‌‌​‌‌​​​‌​‌​​​​​​​
